reviewHtml:
The weird simplicity of Matt Empringham and Freddy Coombes’s A Letter collection took its first turn on a runway at London Fashion Week. All fresh summer frocks, a-line elasticated-waist skirts, straightforward shirts, and puffy satin mini shifts, here was something brimming with a very English sort of deliberate naïveté. A knowingly cheerful reveling in the home-made, the sensibly wearable, and the apparently artifice-free.

By a very odd coincidence, the pair of friends said they’d taken vintage garments with the St Michael label as one of their building blocks. “You can buy a lot on Vinted,” Empringham remarked in a preview. That’s where they took the pattern of their summer frock, with its two droopy patch-pockets, from, as well as the perfectly retro floral-printed cotton bra and knickers. In some strange serendipity of London Fashion Week planning, A Letter was showing hours after Marks & Spencer, the high street giant which once branded all their clothing St Michael from the 1950s to the ’80s, had staged a mega-show in celebration of its 100th anniversary.

But this was a micro-show that all fashion insiders were just as riveted by. This young pair of friends, who bonded while at Central Saint Martins during the lockdown years and started making things together at the age of 22, have built up a crowd of curious fans—international ones too—for their brightly colored one-dimensional paper garments. This was all thanks to Dover Street Market’s willingness to display A Letter work that begged the question: Was it art or fashion, or fashion-as-art, or just a couple of kids messing around making cardboard polo shirts?

“We’ve never actually shown anything on a body before, because it’s always been flat,” said Empringham, speaking with Coombes in the tiny studio they’ve been occupying for the last two years at the Sarabande Foundation, a space just large enough for a desk, two chairs, and the domestic sewing machine they bought with money from the BFC’s New Gen scheme. “There’s definitely a desire to to to really make clothes now,” said Coombes. “We were for quite a while making objects. So the clothes all work in movement, and this is the first thing we’ve done that’s physically moving. The previous shows that we’ve done have all been photo shoots or exhibitions.”

They picked out three generic garments to draw from: a donkey jacket, a Ben Sherman-type shirt, and the St Michael dress. At root, they’re all stalwart signifiers of British working class heritage, a “normal” way of 20th century life that’s now passed, for good or bad. A Letter’s show floated above the deeper possible meanings, coming over as fresh, young, and highly intentional. Everything was made by them in their box of a studio: “We didn’t want the look of something factory-made,” said Empringham. “We thought it was nice to leave in the sort of strange imperfections; we tried to sort of cling onto that pattern-wise and fit-wise.” Coombes added: “That definitely gave the looks, in our opinion, a bit of character.”

In a small collection, there was a lot of rotation of the same shapes—a rule-breaker in normal fashion shows—but their point, well proved, was how very different their things looked in different fabrics. Red and white checked gingham hangs very differently from skimpy silk, which again is nothing like crispy lime green neon nylon.

Backstage afterwards—also a tiny space at Rose Easton Gallery—the designers were trying to get a glass of prosecco, before realizing they needed to do their first post-show de-briefing to a throng of journalists first. How was the show for them? “Well, we were dressing and changing all the models ourselves,” Empringham laughed. “It was chaos.”
